newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Macraes sees sharp yr profit fall.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Macraes sees sharp yr profit fall.

text.p: New Zealand gold miner Macraes Mining Company Ltd will post a sharply lower profit in the year to December 1997, managing director Patrick O'Connor said on Tuesday.

In an interview with Reuters, O'Connor said the company had postponed expansion plans because of a slump in the price of gold, but was well placed to weather the doldrums while others could be put out of business.
"We're forecasting (1997) production at 120,000 ounces currently, down from 138,000 last year," said O'Connor.
On that basis, he said, brokers were predicting a pre-tax profit of between NZ$8 million and $10 million for the year, down from $23.6 million in 1996.
"I think that's realistic. We had a disappointing first quarter this year. The second the quarter has probably been okay. But 120,000 (ounces) is within the production ball park."

O'Connor said the lower profit was a result of the reduced amount and lower grade of gold being extracted from the Macraes mine, which lies near the South Island city of Dunedin at the southern end of New Zealand's South Island.
The company had been gearing up to invest $120 million in the mine and expand its production to nine million tonnes of gold a year from three million tonnes, or about 120,000 ounces.
But the sharp fall in the price of gold in July this year, and a delay in securing local government resource consents, had forced Macraes to shelve its plans and review operations.
O'Connor said about 50 redundancies would be announced.

"The reason for this expenditure review is to look at the cost of the three million tonne business to protect profitability until such time as we get the consents and a change in the gold price," O'Connor said.

An ounce of gold costs about US$320 today compared with over US$400 a year ago. In July the Reserve bank of Australia sold 167 tonnes of gold, sending the price from around US$335 an ounce down to below US$318.
O'Connor said Macraes was fortunate to have good hedging cover in place, with 770,000 ounces of gold forward sold, which would help it to maintain profitability during gold's lull.
"If we up the plant capacity to nine million tonnes (over 300,000 ounces a year), you'd have less than three years worth of hedging," O'Connor said.

"Whereas at three million tonnes in a low gold price environment we have six-plus years of hedging, which is obviously very attractive given that most mining companies around the world would have less than two."

O'Connor said the gold mining industry was in dire straits, and many companies would be forced to close mines over the next six months. But this could be beneficial in that it would curtail supply and increase demand.

"They're talking about 25 mines in Australia potentially closing, they're talked about 10,000 redundancies in WA (Western Australia), and they're talking about 50 percent of South African production being uneconomic," he said.

"So within a fairly short period or time, production will decrease as these mines run out of hedging. You will see mines close over the next six months, and that will contract supply. In a normal world, one would think the (gold) price would go up after that."
O'Connor said Macraes was in a strong financial position, with no debt and $25 million in cash reserves as at June 30.
But he said a significant amount of money had been spent on preparation for the expansion and the company now needed to review its growth strategy and overheads with a new timetable.
Macraes was confident the price of gold would recover in the next 12 months, allowing the expansion to go ahead.

"We're in a very good position to survive and there will be players who don't survive this current price decrease," O'Connor said. "I think the strong companies are going to be the companies without debt, with cash and good hedging."
